80403.subject: What actually outruns Bitcoin?
80403.body:
View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/eaa70932-7ce4-467e-b338-a662ed575d6a/0xR_NL_Banner_Heading_Wordmark.jpg?t=1776775276)
Caption: 

BTC lost more than half its value since its peak in October 202 and has rallied 46.8% since its June 30 low, just short of a formal bull leg. ETH and SOL fell harder than BTC on the way down, and the question is whether anything outruns it on the way up (without any external leverage). Our candidate set is the ten instruments seen below.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/d6180e5c-ad43-43d4-8043-93a891523774/image.png?t=1791377937)
Caption: 

We run two tests

1. Weekly beta to BTC split into upside and downside

2. Each candidate's return against BTC across six bull legs and nine drawdowns since March 2020.

As shown below, only ETH, SOL, MSTR and COIN have a 2Y beta to BTC that sits reliably above 1 alongside BTC explaining most of their moves. Miners are volatile but not much tied to BTC (at least not since their AI pivots). 

ETH and SOL give back more in BTC sell-offs than they add in rallies. Though for ETH, the gap has narrowed lately, with ETH's 1Y split at 1.39 vs. 1.48. MSTR is symmetric at 1.23 on both sides over 2Y and HYPE actually outperforms (slightly) on the way up and (materially) on the way down though with an R² of 0.18 it’s too noisy to rank. 

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/409be9a9-0ff7-495f-88df-bf4f1f1013dd/image.png?t=1791377938)
Caption: 

ETH, SOL and HYPE betas have cooled from their late 2025 peaks to about 1.2, so the amplification is real but smaller than a year ago.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/9fbabedd-07b6-4b1a-9dc0-48f1efa5ac3d/image.png?t=1791377938)
Caption: 

MSTR's beta is rising to its highest reading since 2021 while RIOT's slips below 1, so treasury equities are amplifying BTC more than miners are. MSTR's beta is the strongest current signal, which makes sense as it reflects corporate leverage and the mNAV premium.

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b77ab360-4cca-4428-a33e-db5d18d02e52/image.png?t=1791377939)
Caption: 

Now for test two: bull- and bear-market behaviour. We count a bull leg as any BTC rally of 50% or more between 25% reversals in daily closes, which gives six complete legs since March 2020. No candidate beat BTC in all of them. SOL came closest, beating BTC in four of five legs with a median multiple of 3.54x. MARA and RIOT won four of six (medians of 1.62x and 1.68x), ETH three of six (1.06x) and MSTR two of five (0.64x).

80401.subject: AI Ambition Is Cheap;Why Isolated AI Tools Break at Enterprise Scale; Most companies don’t have an AI agent problem. They have an architecture problem
80401.body:
AI Frontier

Автор: Steve Nouri


Автор: Steve Nouri

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/ai-ambition-cheapwhy-isolated-tools-break-enterprise-scale-nouri-im6fc?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3Bz6qJ1hSFQxeYWgJkQ0HHjg%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=3JJmm0JEtdAIs1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~muy574ra~10-null-null&eid=fz96fz-muy574ra-10
  
Generative and agentic AI have made experimentation easier than ever, but launching pilots is not the same as creating business value. The real divide is now between companies that test AI and companies that can repeatedly build, deploy, adopt, and scale it. Most wining companies that I talked with concentrated their transformation on three or fewer priority areas. They did not spread AI across the organization. They focused resources where the economic impact was highest. That is the first lesson: stop collecting use cases. Many companies deploy copilots, agents, and automation tools inside existing processes. This may improve individual tasks, but it rarely changes the economics of the business. The larger opportunity is to redesign complete workflows. Instead of asking how AI can accelerate one step in claims processing, supply-chain planning, customer support, or software development, leaders should ask what the entire process would look like if it were rebuilt around AI. McKinsey found that reimagining workflows end to end had one of the strongest correlations with value. The second lesson is that AI transformation is a people transformation. Agents may take over routine execution, coordination, and some decision-making, but this changes human roles rather than removing the need for strong teams. Companies must redesign responsibilities, retrain employees, and combine human judgment with machine execution. The third lesson is speed. DBS once needed 18 months to put its first AI model into production. It can now deploy one every two months. The advantage is not any single model. It is the organizational system that allows the company to keep moving faster. Finally, AI cannot be delegated to the technology department. Successful transformation requires the CEO to make it a top priority, while business leaders, finance, HR, product, and technology teams share responsibility for delivery. AI becomes valuable when the business owns the outcome, not when IT owns another project. The companies winning with AI are not necessarily using the most advanced models. They are choosing fewer priorities, redesigning complete workflows, preparing people for adoption, and building the ability to move from idea to impact repeatedly. AI ambition gets attention.
